{{infobox religious building |name=Utaki }} {{Short description|Sacred place in Ryukyuan religion}} {{Unreferenced stub|auto=yes|date=December 2009}} {{For|the album by [[Misako Odani]] of the same name|Utaki (album)}} [[Image:Sefautaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|Sefa-utaki]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽) is an [[Okinawan language|Okinawan]] term for a sacred place, often a grove, cave, or mountain. They are central to the [[Ryukyuan religion]] and the former [[Noro (priestess)|noro priestess]] system. Although the term ''utaki'' is used throughout the [[Ryukyu Islands]], the terms ''suku'' and ''on'' are heard in the [[Miyako-jima|Miyako]] and [[Yaeyama Islands|Yaeyama]] regions respectively. Utaki are usually located on the outskirts of villages and are places for the veneration of gods and ancestors. Most [[gusuku]] have places of worship, and it is theorized that the origins of both ''gusuku'' and ''utaki'' are closely related.
==Overview==
==Important Utaki== * [[Biinudaki]] ([[弁ヶ嶽]]), [[Naha, Okinawa|Naha]] * [[Misaki-on]] ([[美崎御嶽]]), [[Ishigaki, Okinawa|Ishigaki]] * [[Miyatori-on]] (宮鳥御嶽), [[Nago, Okinawa|Nago]] * [[Pyarumizu-utaki]] (漲水御嶽), [[Miyakojima, Okinawa|Miyako]] * [[Sefa-utaki]] (斎場御嶽), [[Nanjo, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * [[Sunuhyan-utaki]] ([[園比屋武御嶽]]), Naha * [[Tohaya-uganju]] ([[渡波屋拝所]]), Nago * [[Tsunoji-utaki]] ([[ツノジ御嶽]]), Miyako * [[Upugusuku-utaki]] ([[大城御嶽]]), Miyako
{{Source|date=November 6, 2013 (Wed) 01:27 (UTC)}} [[File:Sangui (Triangle Rock) of Sefa-Utaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Sangui (Sangūi)]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽, '''Utaki''') is a sacred site for rituals in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, also known as "Kusatimui" (腰当森) or "Ogami-yama" (拝み山).
== Overview == Utaki is a general term for sacred sites in the {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established during the {{ill|Ryukyu Kingdom|ja|琉球王国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Second Shō dynasty|ja|第二尚氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Before this, various regional names existed. The term "Utaki" is primarily used on {{ill|Okinawa Island|ja|沖縄本島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and surrounding islands, but other areas have unique names: - {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: "Suku" (すく) - {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: ** "On" (おん) on {{ill|Ishigaki Island|ja|石垣島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Taketomi Island|ja|竹富島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Ugan" (うがん) on {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Wan" (わん) on {{ill|Kuroshima|ja|黒島 (沖縄県竹富町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kohama Island|ja|小浜島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Waa" (わー) on {{ill|Hateruma Island|ja|波照間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
=== Position in Belief === Utaki are sites where deities from Ryukyuan mythology reside or visit, and they are centers of ancestor worship. They remain important places of worship, believed to protect the region. Since women traditionally serve as priests in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Utaki were strictly {{ill|Nyonin_Kinsei#Danshi_Kinsei_(Men_are_forbidden)|ja|男子禁制|lt=Danshi Kinsei (Men are forbidden)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the kingdom era. Even today, many allow only limited male access.
=== Form and Structure === [[File:Utaki.JPG|right|thumb|An Utaki at {{ill|Okinawa Commemorative National Government Park|ja|国営沖縄記念公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] Utaki are often natural spaces, such as forests, springs, or rivers; some encompass entire islands. Many have a stone monument called "Ibe" or "Ibi-ishi," marking the site where a deity is believed to descend. Although not originally considered sacred objects, some are now treated as such. In the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is common for Utaki to be established on the tombs of past {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, revered as guardian deities.
Large Utaki may include spaces called "Kami-ashagi" (神あしゃぎ, 神あさげ), meaning "God's resting place," where songs and dances are performed to welcome the gods. The term originates from "Kami-ashi-age," meaning a place where the gods 'raise their feet' (sit down).
==== Torii at Utaki and Gusuku ==== [[Torii]] gates, commonly associated with Shinto shrines, are found at the entrances of some Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) in modern Okinawa. However, torii were not part of traditional Ryukyuan Utaki. The notable exception was {{ill|Naminoue Shrine|ja|波上宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which included torii from its inception during King {{ill|Satto|ja|察度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s era when Shinto deities were enshrined.
The presence of torii is attributed to the [[Japanization|kōminka policy]] following the {{ill|Ryukyu Disposition|ja|琉球処分|qq=draft|qq=draft}} after the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Under initiatives like the "One Village, One Shrine" policy, many Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were converted into Shinto shrines.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Junhito Kaji|title=History and Uniqueness of Okinawan Shrines|journal=Nihon Jomin Bunka Kenkyujo|volume=16|year=2018|pages=37-68|url=https://kanagawa-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/12658}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Was Sefa-utaki almost turned into a shrine? – Nanjō Digital Archive|url=https://nanjo-archive.jp/feature/615/|accessdate=2023-06-02}}</ref>
For example, at {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a torii was installed in 1930 (Shōwa 5) but was removed in 2003 (Heisei 15) after the site was designated a component of the [[UNESCO World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage]]-listed "{{ill|Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu|ja|琉球王国のグスク及び関連遺産群|qq=draft|qq=draft}}," to restore its original landscape.
However, torii installed post-annexation remain at sites like {{ill|Nago Castle|ja|名護城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tana Shrine|ja|田名神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Iheya Island|ja|伊平屋島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Arahari Utaki|ja|阿良御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Ie Island|ja|伊江島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyako and Yaeyama), most torii remain intact. == Origins == [[File:Ufuuri.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ufugui (大庫理)]] It is widely believed that Utaki were originally sites of ancient settlements. This theory is supported by numerous discoveries of {{ill|Human remains|ja|遺骨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} near Utaki, indicating their close ties to {{ill|Ancestor worship|ja|祖先崇拝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Additionally, many rivers and springs are considered Utaki or sacred spaces of equal importance, as ancient societies revered water sources due to Okinawa’s porous {{ill|Ryukyu limestone|ja|琉球石灰岩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which made water precious and sacred.<ref name=":0">[https://ja.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%BE%A1%E5%B6%BD_(%E6%B2%96%E7%B8%84)&oldid=103787365 Ontake (Okinawa) - Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia]</ref>
Many {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) feature {{ill|Haisho#Uganju|lt=Uganju (place of worship)|ja|拝所|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. This has led some scholars to argue that Gusuku were originally settlements centered around Utaki, which later developed into fortresses. Certain castles, such as {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were themselves regarded as Utaki.<ref name=":0" />
== Modern Status == Ryukyuan faith remains deeply rooted in the local community, with many Utaki still serving as vital spiritual centers, often maintained by the community or female priests known as {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Some Utaki, like {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, have become popular tourist attractions, though these are rare examples. Most remain primarily places of local worship and pilgrimage, such as those visited during the {{ill|Agari-umai|ja|東御廻り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Nakijin-nubui|ja|今帰仁上り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} pilgrimages.
However, some Utaki have been destroyed or restricted due to {{ill|United States military occupation of Okinawa|ja|アメリカ合衆国による沖縄統治|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, archaeological excavations, or development projects. For example, several Utaki within the {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} grounds were accessible for worshippers before the castle’s reconstruction, but later became off-limits or subject to paid entry.
== Major Utaki == Below is a list of notable Utaki significant in Ryukyuan faith. While most ancient {{ill|Settlements|ja|集落|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Ryukyu Kingdom had at least one Utaki, the following are only select prominent examples.
=== Ryukyu Creation Nine Sacred Utaki (琉球開闢九御嶽) === Ryukyuan mythology states that {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the creator deity, was commanded by the {{ill|Sun deity|ja|太陽神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to create islands, forming Okinawa and establishing nine sacred sites.<ref>"{{ill|Chūzan Seikan|ja|中山世鑑|qq=draft|qq=draft}}"</ref><ref>"Records of {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ceremony"</ref> Seven of these remain revered as the most sacred Utaki.
The most significant under the kingdom's theocratic system was {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where the {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s inauguration ceremonies were held. From Sefa-utaki, {{ill|Kudaka Island|ja|久高島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the landing site of {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, can be worshipped, although this practice is undocumented in historical records. During royal enthronements, the {{ill|Kimitezuri|ja|君手摩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ritual required visiting five Utaki, ending at {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
List of the Nine Sacred Utaki in creation order: * {{ill|Asumui Utaki|ja|安須森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Kunigami, Okinawa|Kunigami]] * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Nakijin Castle|Nakijin Gusuku]], [[Nakijin, Okinawa|Nakijin]] * Chinen-mori: [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Chinen * {{ill|Yabusatsu Utaki|ja|薮薩御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsuzu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku, within {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * {{ill|Kubou Utaki (Kudaka Island)|ja|クボー御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Kudaka Island * Shurimui Utaki: One of Shuri’s Ten Sacred Sites * {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Shuri Castle
The {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was lost during the Battle of Okinawa and later reconstruction work at Shuri Castle. Entry to its former site is now prohibited. ``` === Higashi-umari Utaki (Eastern Pilgrimage Utaki) === [[File:Sonohyan-utaki.jpeg|right|thumb|{{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, behind the stone gate]] The Higashi-umari (あがりうまーい) is a [[pilgrimage|sacred pilgrimage]] still practiced today, where pilgrims visit utaki in Tamagusuku, Chinen, Sashiki, and Ōzato—regions considered sacred because they lie east of Shuri, the direction where the sun rises and where {{ill|Niraikanai|ja|ニライカナイ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} is believed to exist.
The pilgrimage originated as a ritual of the Ryukyu king, but over time, it spread to the aristocracy and the common people. Today, it is mainly performed by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). Although the pilgrimage route varies slightly by clan, it generally starts from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and follows this order:
* {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (すぬひゃんうたき): Outside [[Shuri Castle]] * Yonabaru Oyagaa (与那原親川, よなばるうぇーがー): [[Yonabaru, Okinawa|Yonabaru Town]] * Udunyama (御殿山, うどぅんやま): Yonabaru Town * Baten Utaki (場天御嶽, ばてぃんうたき): {{ill|Sashiki, Okinawa|ja|佐敷町 (沖縄県)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō City]] * Sashiki Uigusuku (佐敷上グスク, さしきうぃぐすく): Nanjō City, Sashiki * Tida Ugā (テダ御川, てぃだうかー): {{ill|Chinen, Okinawa|ja|知念村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (せーふぁうたき): Nanjō City, Chinen * Tomui Utaki (友利ノ御嶽, とむいのたけ): Chinen Gusuku, Nanjō City * Chinen Ukkā (知念大川, ちねんうっかー): Nanjō City, Chinen * Mintongusuku (ミントングスク, みんとぅんぐすく): {{ill|Tamagusuku, Okinawa|ja|玉城村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * Nakandakari Hīja (仲村渠樋川, なかんだかりひーじゃー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Aihanta Utaki (アイハンタ御嶽, あいはんたうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yabusatsu Utaki (藪薩御嶽, やぶさつうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yahara Tsukasa (ヤハラヅカサ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Supana Tsukasa (潮花司, すーぱなつかさ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Utaki (浜川御嶽, はまがーうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Ukijuhainju (浜川受水走水, はまがーうきんじゅはいんじゅ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsudu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (あまつづてんつぎうたき): In {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ruins * Tamagusuku Nunduchi (玉城祝女殿内, たまぐすくぬんどぅち): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Shichinbaru Jingaa (志堅原仁川, しちんばるじんがー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku
=== Nakijin-nobori Utaki (Nakijin Ascension Utaki) === The Nakijin-nobori (なきじんぬぶい) pilgrimage is a sacred journey centered on utaki in the Nakijin region. It is primarily conducted by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). The origins are unclear, but Nakijin, the former capital of the Northern Kingdom (Hokuzan), holds significant historical importance as the birthplace of many Ryukyuan noble lineages. The route and utaki visited vary by clan, but the main sites are:
* Karaukā (カラウカー): Inside {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Hino-kami no Hokora (火の神の祠): Inside Nakijin Castle * Tenchigi Utaki (テンチギの御嶽, also called Kanahiyabu): The second utaki created at Nakijin * Soitsugi Utaki (ソイツギの御嶽): Inside Nakijin Castle * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Inside Nakijin Castle * Aoriyahe Noro Nunduchi (阿応理屋恵祝女殿内, あおりやへのろどぅんち): In {{ill|Nakijin Village|ja|今帰仁村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Nakijin Noro Nunduchi (今帰仁祝女殿内, なきじんのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Tumu no Kane Noro Hino-kami (供のカネー祝女火の神, とぅむなはーにーのろひぬかん): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Oyagaa (今泊の親川, えーがー): Nakijin Village * Nakagusuku Noro Nunduchi (中城祝女殿内, なかぐすくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Tsuya-guchi-baka (今泊の津屋口墓, ちぇーぐちばか): Nakijin Village * Shoshi Akaubaka (諸志の赤御墓, あかうばか): Nakijin Village * Ichigusuku Baka (池城墓, いちぐすくばか): Nakijin Village * Ōnishi Baka (大北墓, うーにしばか, also called Aji Ubaka): Nakijin Village * Momujana Baka (百按司墓, むむじゃなばか): Nakijin Village * Tiragama (ティラガマ): Nakijin Village * Jitchaku Noro Nunduchi (勢理客祝女殿内, じっちゃくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village
=== Sakishima Islands Utaki === The {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which include the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, are home to many ancient sacred sites predating Ryukyuan control. In the Yaeyama Islands, utaki are often called "on" or "wan." Below are some notable examples:
==== Miyako Islands ==== [[File:Miyako harimizu utaki.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ぴゃるみずうたき, はりみずうたき) : [[Miyakojima]] ({{ill|Miyakojima City|ja|宮古島市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). This utaki is dedicated to Koitsuno (古意角) and Koitama (姑依玉), the deities who created Miyako Island. Other deities include the Ryūgū-shin (Dragon Palace God) and the island guardian deity Kokatamotenfū. The surrounding stone walls were built by {{ill|Nakasone Tuyumya|ja|仲宗根豊見親|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to commemorate his victory in the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in 1500. ; Shimajiri Motoshima (島尻元島) : Miyakojima City, Hirara Shimajiri. The site is central to the unique local festival {{ill|Paantu|ja|パーントゥ・プナハ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; Ūparu Utaki (大主御嶽, ウパルズ御嶽, ナナムイ) : {{ill|Ikema Island|ja|池間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyakojima City). Also known as Ōnushi Shrine, this utaki enshrines Uraserikutamenauno Manus, the guardian deity of Ikema people. Immigrants from Ikema established related utaki on {{ill|Irabu Island|ja|伊良部島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Nishihara.
==== Yaeyama Islands ==== [[File:Misaki-On Ishigakijima01s3s4592.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Maitsuba Utaki|ja|真乙姥御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (まいつばおん) : [[Ishigaki Island]] ({{ill|Ishigaki City|ja|石垣市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to a priestess who played a role in the suppression of the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (みしゃぎおん) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). It is a designated {{ill|Cultural Property of Okinawa Prefecture|ja|沖縄県指定文化財一覧|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Ninibushi Utaki|ja|群星御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (んにぶしおん, んにぶしうたき) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). Center of the festival {{ill|Mayunganaashi|ja|マユンガナシ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Nishitō Utaki|ja|西塘御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (にしとうおん) : [[Taketomi Island]] ({{ill|Taketomi Town|ja|竹富町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to {{ill|Nishitō|ja|西塘|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a Yaeyama lord, and designated an Okinawa Prefectural Historic Site. ; {{ill|Kuninaka Utaki|ja|国仲御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふいなーおん, くになかうたき) : Taketomi Island. It is the only utaki in Yaeyama directly connected to the Ryukyu royal family, having received a deity from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Sanri Utaki|ja|三離御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふなふら, みちゃーりおん, さんりうたき) : [[Iriomote Island]] (Taketomi Town, Komi). It shares significance with {{ill|Akamata-Kuromata Festival|ja|アカマタ・クロマタ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Toyama Utaki|ja|十山御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (とぅやまうがん) : [[Yonaguni Island]] ({{ill|Yonaguni Town|ja|与那国町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sonai|ja|祖納|qq=draft|qq=draft}}).
=== Amami Islands === The {{ill|Amami Islands|ja|奄美群島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also had a {{ill|Noro (priestess)|lt=Noro system|ja|ノロ制度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, but there were no {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|qq=draft|qq=draft}} specifically called "utaki" (御嶽). However, sacred sites similar to {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, known as {{ill|Amandee|ja|アマンデー|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (奄美嶽, 海見嶽), do exist. Other sacred places include mountains known as "Ogami-yama" (拝み山) and rock formations called "Tategami" (立神).
Many sites with names like {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine|ja|厳島神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Takachiho Shrine|ja|高千穂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are believed to be utaki-style places of worship rather than standard Shinto shrines. It is thought that these sacred places were converted into Shinto shrines during the rule of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{infobox religious building |name=Utaki }} {{Short description|Sacred place in Ryukyuan religion}} {{Unreferenced stub|auto=yes|date=December 2009}} {{For|the album by [[Misako Odani]] of the same name|Utaki (album)}} [[Image:Sefautaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|Sefa-utaki]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽) is an [[Okinawan language|Okinawan]] term for a sacred place, often a grove, cave, or mountain. They are central to the [[Ryukyuan religion]] and the former [[Noro (priestess)|noro priestess]] system. Although the term ''utaki'' is used throughout the [[Ryukyu Islands]], the terms ''suku'' and ''on'' are heard in the [[Miyako-jima|Miyako]] and [[Yaeyama Islands|Yaeyama]] regions respectively. Utaki are usually located on the outskirts of villages and are places for the veneration of gods and ancestors. Most [[gusuku]] have places of worship, and it is theorized that the origins of both ''gusuku'' and ''utaki'' are closely related.
==Overview==
==Important Utaki== * [[Biinudaki]] ([[弁ヶ嶽]]), [[Naha, Okinawa|Naha]] * [[Misaki-on]] ([[美崎御嶽]]), [[Ishigaki, Okinawa|Ishigaki]] * [[Miyatori-on]] (宮鳥御嶽), [[Nago, Okinawa|Nago]] * [[Pyarumizu-utaki]] (漲水御嶽), [[Miyakojima, Okinawa|Miyako]] * [[Sefa-utaki]] (斎場御嶽), [[Nanjo, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * [[Sunuhyan-utaki]] ([[園比屋武御嶽]]), Naha * [[Tohaya-uganju]] ([[渡波屋拝所]]), Nago * [[Tsunoji-utaki]] ([[ツノジ御嶽]]), Miyako * [[Upugusuku-utaki]] ([[大城御嶽]]), Miyako
{{Source|date=November 6, 2013 (Wed) 01:27 (UTC)}} [[File:Sangui (Triangle Rock) of Sefa-Utaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Sangui (Sangūi)]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽, '''Utaki''') is a sacred site for rituals in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, also known as "Kusatimui" (腰当森) or "Ogami-yama" (拝み山).
== Overview == Utaki is a general term for sacred sites in the {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established during the {{ill|Ryukyu Kingdom|ja|琉球王国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Second Shō dynasty|ja|第二尚氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Before this, various regional names existed. The term "Utaki" is primarily used on {{ill|Okinawa Island|ja|沖縄本島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and surrounding islands, but other areas have unique names: - {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: "Suku" (すく) - {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: ** "On" (おん) on {{ill|Ishigaki Island|ja|石垣島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Taketomi Island|ja|竹富島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Ugan" (うがん) on {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Wan" (わん) on {{ill|Kuroshima|ja|黒島 (沖縄県竹富町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kohama Island|ja|小浜島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Waa" (わー) on {{ill|Hateruma Island|ja|波照間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
=== Position in Belief === Utaki are sites where deities from Ryukyuan mythology reside or visit, and they are centers of ancestor worship. They remain important places of worship, believed to protect the region. Since women traditionally serve as priests in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Utaki were strictly {{ill|Nyonin_Kinsei#Danshi_Kinsei_(Men_are_forbidden)|ja|男子禁制|lt=Danshi Kinsei (Men are forbidden)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the kingdom era. Even today, many allow only limited male access.
=== Form and Structure === [[File:Utaki.JPG|right|thumb|An Utaki at {{ill|Okinawa Commemorative National Government Park|ja|国営沖縄記念公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] Utaki are often natural spaces, such as forests, springs, or rivers; some encompass entire islands. Many have a stone monument called "Ibe" or "Ibi-ishi," marking the site where a deity is believed to descend. Although not originally considered sacred objects, some are now treated as such. In the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is common for Utaki to be established on the tombs of past {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, revered as guardian deities.
Large Utaki may include spaces called "Kami-ashagi" (神あしゃぎ, 神あさげ), meaning "God's resting place," where songs and dances are performed to welcome the gods. The term originates from "Kami-ashi-age," meaning a place where the gods 'raise their feet' (sit down).
==== Torii at Utaki and Gusuku ==== [[Torii]] gates, commonly associated with Shinto shrines, are found at the entrances of some Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) in modern Okinawa. However, torii were not part of traditional Ryukyuan Utaki. The notable exception was {{ill|Naminoue Shrine|ja|波上宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which included torii from its inception during King {{ill|Satto|ja|察度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s era when Shinto deities were enshrined.
The presence of torii is attributed to the [[Japanization|kōminka policy]] following the {{ill|Ryukyu Disposition|ja|琉球処分|qq=draft|qq=draft}} after the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Under initiatives like the "One Village, One Shrine" policy, many Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were converted into Shinto shrines.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Junhito Kaji|title=History and Uniqueness of Okinawan Shrines|journal=Nihon Jomin Bunka Kenkyujo|volume=16|year=2018|pages=37-68|url=https://kanagawa-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/12658}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Was Sefa-utaki almost turned into a shrine? – Nanjō Digital Archive|url=https://nanjo-archive.jp/feature/615/|accessdate=2023-06-02}}</ref>
For example, at {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a torii was installed in 1930 (Shōwa 5) but was removed in 2003 (Heisei 15) after the site was designated a component of the [[UNESCO World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage]]-listed "{{ill|Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu|ja|琉球王国のグスク及び関連遺産群|qq=draft|qq=draft}}," to restore its original landscape.
However, torii installed post-annexation remain at sites like {{ill|Nago Castle|ja|名護城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tana Shrine|ja|田名神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Iheya Island|ja|伊平屋島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Arahari Utaki|ja|阿良御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Ie Island|ja|伊江島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyako and Yaeyama), most torii remain intact. == Origins == [[File:Ufuuri.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ufugui (大庫理)]] It is widely believed that Utaki were originally sites of ancient settlements. This theory is supported by numerous discoveries of {{ill|Human remains|ja|遺骨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} near Utaki, indicating their close ties to {{ill|Ancestor worship|ja|祖先崇拝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Additionally, many rivers and springs are considered Utaki or sacred spaces of equal importance, as ancient societies revered water sources due to Okinawa’s porous {{ill|Ryukyu limestone|ja|琉球石灰岩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which made water precious and sacred.<ref name=":0">[https://ja.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%BE%A1%E5%B6%BD_(%E6%B2%96%E7%B8%84)&oldid=103787365 Ontake (Okinawa) - Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia]</ref>
Many {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) feature {{ill|Haisho#Uganju|lt=Uganju (place of worship)|ja|拝所|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. This has led some scholars to argue that Gusuku were originally settlements centered around Utaki, which later developed into fortresses. Certain castles, such as {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were themselves regarded as Utaki.<ref name=":0" />
== Modern Status == Ryukyuan faith remains deeply rooted in the local community, with many Utaki still serving as vital spiritual centers, often maintained by the community or female priests known as {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Some Utaki, like {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, have become popular tourist attractions, though these are rare examples. Most remain primarily places of local worship and pilgrimage, such as those visited during the {{ill|Agari-umai|ja|東御廻り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Nakijin-nubui|ja|今帰仁上り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} pilgrimages.
However, some Utaki have been destroyed or restricted due to {{ill|United States military occupation of Okinawa|ja|アメリカ合衆国による沖縄統治|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, archaeological excavations, or development projects. For example, several Utaki within the {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} grounds were accessible for worshippers before the castle’s reconstruction, but later became off-limits or subject to paid entry.
== Major Utaki == Below is a list of notable Utaki significant in Ryukyuan faith. While most ancient {{ill|Settlements|ja|集落|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Ryukyu Kingdom had at least one Utaki, the following are only select prominent examples.
=== Ryukyu Creation Nine Sacred Utaki (琉球開闢九御嶽) === Ryukyuan mythology states that {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the creator deity, was commanded by the {{ill|Sun deity|ja|太陽神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to create islands, forming Okinawa and establishing nine sacred sites.<ref>"{{ill|Chūzan Seikan|ja|中山世鑑|qq=draft|qq=draft}}"</ref><ref>"Records of {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ceremony"</ref> Seven of these remain revered as the most sacred Utaki.
The most significant under the kingdom's theocratic system was {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where the {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s inauguration ceremonies were held. From Sefa-utaki, {{ill|Kudaka Island|ja|久高島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the landing site of {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, can be worshipped, although this practice is undocumented in historical records. During royal enthronements, the {{ill|Kimitezuri|ja|君手摩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ritual required visiting five Utaki, ending at {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
List of the Nine Sacred Utaki in creation order: * {{ill|Asumui Utaki|ja|安須森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Kunigami, Okinawa|Kunigami]] * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Nakijin Castle|Nakijin Gusuku]], [[Nakijin, Okinawa|Nakijin]] * Chinen-mori: [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Chinen * {{ill|Yabusatsu Utaki|ja|薮薩御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsuzu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku, within {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * {{ill|Kubou Utaki (Kudaka Island)|ja|クボー御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Kudaka Island * Shurimui Utaki: One of Shuri’s Ten Sacred Sites * {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Shuri Castle
The {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was lost during the Battle of Okinawa and later reconstruction work at Shuri Castle. Entry to its former site is now prohibited. ``` === Higashi-umari Utaki (Eastern Pilgrimage Utaki) === [[File:Sonohyan-utaki.jpeg|right|thumb|{{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, behind the stone gate]] The Higashi-umari (あがりうまーい) is a [[pilgrimage|sacred pilgrimage]] still practiced today, where pilgrims visit utaki in Tamagusuku, Chinen, Sashiki, and Ōzato—regions considered sacred because they lie east of Shuri, the direction where the sun rises and where {{ill|Niraikanai|ja|ニライカナイ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} is believed to exist.
The pilgrimage originated as a ritual of the Ryukyu king, but over time, it spread to the aristocracy and the common people. Today, it is mainly performed by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). Although the pilgrimage route varies slightly by clan, it generally starts from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and follows this order:
* {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (すぬひゃんうたき): Outside [[Shuri Castle]] * Yonabaru Oyagaa (与那原親川, よなばるうぇーがー): [[Yonabaru, Okinawa|Yonabaru Town]] * Udunyama (御殿山, うどぅんやま): Yonabaru Town * Baten Utaki (場天御嶽, ばてぃんうたき): {{ill|Sashiki, Okinawa|ja|佐敷町 (沖縄県)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō City]] * Sashiki Uigusuku (佐敷上グスク, さしきうぃぐすく): Nanjō City, Sashiki * Tida Ugā (テダ御川, てぃだうかー): {{ill|Chinen, Okinawa|ja|知念村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (せーふぁうたき): Nanjō City, Chinen * Tomui Utaki (友利ノ御嶽, とむいのたけ): Chinen Gusuku, Nanjō City * Chinen Ukkā (知念大川, ちねんうっかー): Nanjō City, Chinen * Mintongusuku (ミントングスク, みんとぅんぐすく): {{ill|Tamagusuku, Okinawa|ja|玉城村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * Nakandakari Hīja (仲村渠樋川, なかんだかりひーじゃー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Aihanta Utaki (アイハンタ御嶽, あいはんたうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yabusatsu Utaki (藪薩御嶽, やぶさつうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yahara Tsukasa (ヤハラヅカサ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Supana Tsukasa (潮花司, すーぱなつかさ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Utaki (浜川御嶽, はまがーうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Ukijuhainju (浜川受水走水, はまがーうきんじゅはいんじゅ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsudu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (あまつづてんつぎうたき): In {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ruins * Tamagusuku Nunduchi (玉城祝女殿内, たまぐすくぬんどぅち): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Shichinbaru Jingaa (志堅原仁川, しちんばるじんがー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku
=== Nakijin-nobori Utaki (Nakijin Ascension Utaki) === The Nakijin-nobori (なきじんぬぶい) pilgrimage is a sacred journey centered on utaki in the Nakijin region. It is primarily conducted by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). The origins are unclear, but Nakijin, the former capital of the Northern Kingdom (Hokuzan), holds significant historical importance as the birthplace of many Ryukyuan noble lineages. The route and utaki visited vary by clan, but the main sites are:
* Karaukā (カラウカー): Inside {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Hino-kami no Hokora (火の神の祠): Inside Nakijin Castle * Tenchigi Utaki (テンチギの御嶽, also called Kanahiyabu): The second utaki created at Nakijin * Soitsugi Utaki (ソイツギの御嶽): Inside Nakijin Castle * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Inside Nakijin Castle * Aoriyahe Noro Nunduchi (阿応理屋恵祝女殿内, あおりやへのろどぅんち): In {{ill|Nakijin Village|ja|今帰仁村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Nakijin Noro Nunduchi (今帰仁祝女殿内, なきじんのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Tumu no Kane Noro Hino-kami (供のカネー祝女火の神, とぅむなはーにーのろひぬかん): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Oyagaa (今泊の親川, えーがー): Nakijin Village * Nakagusuku Noro Nunduchi (中城祝女殿内, なかぐすくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Tsuya-guchi-baka (今泊の津屋口墓, ちぇーぐちばか): Nakijin Village * Shoshi Akaubaka (諸志の赤御墓, あかうばか): Nakijin Village * Ichigusuku Baka (池城墓, いちぐすくばか): Nakijin Village * Ōnishi Baka (大北墓, うーにしばか, also called Aji Ubaka): Nakijin Village * Momujana Baka (百按司墓, むむじゃなばか): Nakijin Village * Tiragama (ティラガマ): Nakijin Village * Jitchaku Noro Nunduchi (勢理客祝女殿内, じっちゃくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village
=== Sakishima Islands Utaki === The {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which include the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, are home to many ancient sacred sites predating Ryukyuan control. In the Yaeyama Islands, utaki are often called "on" or "wan." Below are some notable examples:
==== Miyako Islands ==== [[File:Miyako harimizu utaki.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ぴゃるみずうたき, はりみずうたき) : [[Miyakojima]] ({{ill|Miyakojima City|ja|宮古島市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). This utaki is dedicated to Koitsuno (古意角) and Koitama (姑依玉), the deities who created Miyako Island. Other deities include the Ryūgū-shin (Dragon Palace God) and the island guardian deity Kokatamotenfū. The surrounding stone walls were built by {{ill|Nakasone Tuyumya|ja|仲宗根豊見親|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to commemorate his victory in the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in 1500. ; Shimajiri Motoshima (島尻元島) : Miyakojima City, Hirara Shimajiri. The site is central to the unique local festival {{ill|Paantu|ja|パーントゥ・プナハ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; Ūparu Utaki (大主御嶽, ウパルズ御嶽, ナナムイ) : {{ill|Ikema Island|ja|池間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyakojima City). Also known as Ōnushi Shrine, this utaki enshrines Uraserikutamenauno Manus, the guardian deity of Ikema people. Immigrants from Ikema established related utaki on {{ill|Irabu Island|ja|伊良部島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Nishihara.
==== Yaeyama Islands ==== [[File:Misaki-On Ishigakijima01s3s4592.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Maitsuba Utaki|ja|真乙姥御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (まいつばおん) : [[Ishigaki Island]] ({{ill|Ishigaki City|ja|石垣市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to a priestess who played a role in the suppression of the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (みしゃぎおん) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). It is a designated {{ill|Cultural Property of Okinawa Prefecture|ja|沖縄県指定文化財一覧|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Ninibushi Utaki|ja|群星御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (んにぶしおん, んにぶしうたき) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). Center of the festival {{ill|Mayunganaashi|ja|マユンガナシ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Nishitō Utaki|ja|西塘御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (にしとうおん) : [[Taketomi Island]] ({{ill|Taketomi Town|ja|竹富町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to {{ill|Nishitō|ja|西塘|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a Yaeyama lord, and designated an Okinawa Prefectural Historic Site. ; {{ill|Kuninaka Utaki|ja|国仲御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふいなーおん, くになかうたき) : Taketomi Island. It is the only utaki in Yaeyama directly connected to the Ryukyu royal family, having received a deity from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Sanri Utaki|ja|三離御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふなふら, みちゃーりおん, さんりうたき) : [[Iriomote Island]] (Taketomi Town, Komi). It shares significance with {{ill|Akamata-Kuromata Festival|ja|アカマタ・クロマタ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Toyama Utaki|ja|十山御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (とぅやまうがん) : [[Yonaguni Island]] ({{ill|Yonaguni Town|ja|与那国町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sonai|ja|祖納|qq=draft|qq=draft}}).
=== Amami Islands === The {{ill|Amami Islands|ja|奄美群島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also had a {{ill|Noro (priestess)|lt=Noro system|ja|ノロ制度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, but there were no {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|qq=draft|qq=draft}} specifically called "utaki" (御嶽). However, sacred sites similar to {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, known as {{ill|Amandee|ja|アマンデー|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (奄美嶽, 海見嶽), do exist. Other sacred places include mountains known as "Ogami-yama" (拝み山) and rock formations called "Tategami" (立神).
Many sites with names like {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine|ja|厳島神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Takachiho Shrine|ja|高千穂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are believed to be utaki-style places of worship rather than standard Shinto shrines. It is thought that these sacred places were converted into Shinto shrines during the rule of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{infobox religious building |name=Utaki }} {{Short description|Sacred place in Ryukyuan religion}} {{Unreferenced stub|auto=yes|date=December 2009}} {{For|the album by [[Misako Odani]] of the same name|Utaki (album)}} [[Image:Sefautaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|Sefa-utaki]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽) is an [[Okinawan language|Okinawan]] term for a sacred place, often a grove, cave, or mountain. They are central to the [[Ryukyuan religion]] and the former [[Noro (priestess)|noro priestess]] system. Although the term ''utaki'' is used throughout the [[Ryukyu Islands]], the terms ''suku'' and ''on'' are heard in the [[Miyako-jima|Miyako]] and [[Yaeyama Islands|Yaeyama]] regions respectively. Utaki are usually located on the outskirts of villages and are places for the veneration of gods and ancestors. Most [[gusuku]] have places of worship, and it is theorized that the origins of both ''gusuku'' and ''utaki'' are closely related.
==Overview==
==Important Utaki== * [[Biinudaki]] ([[弁ヶ嶽]]), [[Naha, Okinawa|Naha]] * [[Misaki-on]] ([[美崎御嶽]]), [[Ishigaki, Okinawa|Ishigaki]] * [[Miyatori-on]] (宮鳥御嶽), [[Nago, Okinawa|Nago]] * [[Pyarumizu-utaki]] (漲水御嶽), [[Miyakojima, Okinawa|Miyako]] * [[Sefa-utaki]] (斎場御嶽), [[Nanjo, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * [[Sunuhyan-utaki]] ([[園比屋武御嶽]]), Naha * [[Tohaya-uganju]] ([[渡波屋拝所]]), Nago * [[Tsunoji-utaki]] ([[ツノジ御嶽]]), Miyako * [[Upugusuku-utaki]] ([[大城御嶽]]), Miyako
{{Source|date=November 6, 2013 (Wed) 01:27 (UTC)}} [[File:Sangui (Triangle Rock) of Sefa-Utaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Sangui (Sangūi)]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽, '''Utaki''') is a sacred site for rituals in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, also known as "Kusatimui" (腰当森) or "Ogami-yama" (拝み山).
== Overview == Utaki is a general term for sacred sites in the {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established during the {{ill|Ryukyu Kingdom|ja|琉球王国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Second Shō dynasty|ja|第二尚氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Before this, various regional names existed. The term "Utaki" is primarily used on {{ill|Okinawa Island|ja|沖縄本島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and surrounding islands, but other areas have unique names: - {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: "Suku" (すく) - {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: ** "On" (おん) on {{ill|Ishigaki Island|ja|石垣島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Taketomi Island|ja|竹富島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Ugan" (うがん) on {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Wan" (わん) on {{ill|Kuroshima|ja|黒島 (沖縄県竹富町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kohama Island|ja|小浜島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Waa" (わー) on {{ill|Hateruma Island|ja|波照間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
=== Position in Belief === Utaki are sites where deities from Ryukyuan mythology reside or visit, and they are centers of ancestor worship. They remain important places of worship, believed to protect the region. Since women traditionally serve as priests in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Utaki were strictly {{ill|Nyonin_Kinsei#Danshi_Kinsei_(Men_are_forbidden)|ja|男子禁制|lt=Danshi Kinsei (Men are forbidden)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the kingdom era. Even today, many allow only limited male access.
=== Form and Structure === [[File:Utaki.JPG|right|thumb|An Utaki at {{ill|Okinawa Commemorative National Government Park|ja|国営沖縄記念公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] Utaki are often natural spaces, such as forests, springs, or rivers; some encompass entire islands. Many have a stone monument called "Ibe" or "Ibi-ishi," marking the site where a deity is believed to descend. Although not originally considered sacred objects, some are now treated as such. In the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is common for Utaki to be established on the tombs of past {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, revered as guardian deities.
Large Utaki may include spaces called "Kami-ashagi" (神あしゃぎ, 神あさげ), meaning "God's resting place," where songs and dances are performed to welcome the gods. The term originates from "Kami-ashi-age," meaning a place where the gods 'raise their feet' (sit down).
==== Torii at Utaki and Gusuku ==== [[Torii]] gates, commonly associated with Shinto shrines, are found at the entrances of some Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) in modern Okinawa. However, torii were not part of traditional Ryukyuan Utaki. The notable exception was {{ill|Naminoue Shrine|ja|波上宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which included torii from its inception during King {{ill|Satto|ja|察度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s era when Shinto deities were enshrined.
The presence of torii is attributed to the [[Japanization|kōminka policy]] following the {{ill|Ryukyu Disposition|ja|琉球処分|qq=draft|qq=draft}} after the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Under initiatives like the "One Village, One Shrine" policy, many Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were converted into Shinto shrines.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Junhito Kaji|title=History and Uniqueness of Okinawan Shrines|journal=Nihon Jomin Bunka Kenkyujo|volume=16|year=2018|pages=37-68|url=https://kanagawa-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/12658}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Was Sefa-utaki almost turned into a shrine? – Nanjō Digital Archive|url=https://nanjo-archive.jp/feature/615/|accessdate=2023-06-02}}</ref>
For example, at {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a torii was installed in 1930 (Shōwa 5) but was removed in 2003 (Heisei 15) after the site was designated a component of the [[UNESCO World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage]]-listed "{{ill|Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu|ja|琉球王国のグスク及び関連遺産群|qq=draft|qq=draft}}," to restore its original landscape.
However, torii installed post-annexation remain at sites like {{ill|Nago Castle|ja|名護城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tana Shrine|ja|田名神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Iheya Island|ja|伊平屋島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Arahari Utaki|ja|阿良御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Ie Island|ja|伊江島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyako and Yaeyama), most torii remain intact. == Origins == [[File:Ufuuri.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ufugui (大庫理)]] It is widely believed that Utaki were originally sites of ancient settlements. This theory is supported by numerous discoveries of {{ill|Human remains|ja|遺骨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} near Utaki, indicating their close ties to {{ill|Ancestor worship|ja|祖先崇拝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Additionally, many rivers and springs are considered Utaki or sacred spaces of equal importance, as ancient societies revered water sources due to Okinawa’s porous {{ill|Ryukyu limestone|ja|琉球石灰岩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which made water precious and sacred.<ref name=":0">[https://ja.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%BE%A1%E5%B6%BD_(%E6%B2%96%E7%B8%84)&oldid=103787365 Ontake (Okinawa) - Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia]</ref>
Many {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) feature {{ill|Haisho#Uganju|lt=Uganju (place of worship)|ja|拝所|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. This has led some scholars to argue that Gusuku were originally settlements centered around Utaki, which later developed into fortresses. Certain castles, such as {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were themselves regarded as Utaki.<ref name=":0" />
== Modern Status == Ryukyuan faith remains deeply rooted in the local community, with many Utaki still serving as vital spiritual centers, often maintained by the community or female priests known as {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Some Utaki, like {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, have become popular tourist attractions, though these are rare examples. Most remain primarily places of local worship and pilgrimage, such as those visited during the {{ill|Agari-umai|ja|東御廻り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Nakijin-nubui|ja|今帰仁上り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} pilgrimages.
However, some Utaki have been destroyed or restricted due to {{ill|United States military occupation of Okinawa|ja|アメリカ合衆国による沖縄統治|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, archaeological excavations, or development projects. For example, several Utaki within the {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} grounds were accessible for worshippers before the castle’s reconstruction, but later became off-limits or subject to paid entry.
== Major Utaki == Below is a list of notable Utaki significant in Ryukyuan faith. While most ancient {{ill|Settlements|ja|集落|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Ryukyu Kingdom had at least one Utaki, the following are only select prominent examples.
=== Ryukyu Creation Nine Sacred Utaki (琉球開闢九御嶽) === Ryukyuan mythology states that {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the creator deity, was commanded by the {{ill|Sun deity|ja|太陽神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to create islands, forming Okinawa and establishing nine sacred sites.<ref>"{{ill|Chūzan Seikan|ja|中山世鑑|qq=draft|qq=draft}}"</ref><ref>"Records of {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ceremony"</ref> Seven of these remain revered as the most sacred Utaki.
The most significant under the kingdom's theocratic system was {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where the {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s inauguration ceremonies were held. From Sefa-utaki, {{ill|Kudaka Island|ja|久高島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the landing site of {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, can be worshipped, although this practice is undocumented in historical records. During royal enthronements, the {{ill|Kimitezuri|ja|君手摩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ritual required visiting five Utaki, ending at {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
List of the Nine Sacred Utaki in creation order: * {{ill|Asumui Utaki|ja|安須森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Kunigami, Okinawa|Kunigami]] * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Nakijin Castle|Nakijin Gusuku]], [[Nakijin, Okinawa|Nakijin]] * Chinen-mori: [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Chinen * {{ill|Yabusatsu Utaki|ja|薮薩御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsuzu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku, within {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * {{ill|Kubou Utaki (Kudaka Island)|ja|クボー御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Kudaka Island * Shurimui Utaki: One of Shuri’s Ten Sacred Sites * {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Shuri Castle
The {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was lost during the Battle of Okinawa and later reconstruction work at Shuri Castle. Entry to its former site is now prohibited. ``` === Higashi-umari Utaki (Eastern Pilgrimage Utaki) === [[File:Sonohyan-utaki.jpeg|right|thumb|{{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, behind the stone gate]] The Higashi-umari (あがりうまーい) is a [[pilgrimage|sacred pilgrimage]] still practiced today, where pilgrims visit utaki in Tamagusuku, Chinen, Sashiki, and Ōzato—regions considered sacred because they lie east of Shuri, the direction where the sun rises and where {{ill|Niraikanai|ja|ニライカナイ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} is believed to exist.
The pilgrimage originated as a ritual of the Ryukyu king, but over time, it spread to the aristocracy and the common people. Today, it is mainly performed by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). Although the pilgrimage route varies slightly by clan, it generally starts from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and follows this order:
* {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (すぬひゃんうたき): Outside [[Shuri Castle]] * Yonabaru Oyagaa (与那原親川, よなばるうぇーがー): [[Yonabaru, Okinawa|Yonabaru Town]] * Udunyama (御殿山, うどぅんやま): Yonabaru Town * Baten Utaki (場天御嶽, ばてぃんうたき): {{ill|Sashiki, Okinawa|ja|佐敷町 (沖縄県)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō City]] * Sashiki Uigusuku (佐敷上グスク, さしきうぃぐすく): Nanjō City, Sashiki * Tida Ugā (テダ御川, てぃだうかー): {{ill|Chinen, Okinawa|ja|知念村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (せーふぁうたき): Nanjō City, Chinen * Tomui Utaki (友利ノ御嶽, とむいのたけ): Chinen Gusuku, Nanjō City * Chinen Ukkā (知念大川, ちねんうっかー): Nanjō City, Chinen * Mintongusuku (ミントングスク, みんとぅんぐすく): {{ill|Tamagusuku, Okinawa|ja|玉城村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * Nakandakari Hīja (仲村渠樋川, なかんだかりひーじゃー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Aihanta Utaki (アイハンタ御嶽, あいはんたうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yabusatsu Utaki (藪薩御嶽, やぶさつうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yahara Tsukasa (ヤハラヅカサ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Supana Tsukasa (潮花司, すーぱなつかさ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Utaki (浜川御嶽, はまがーうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Ukijuhainju (浜川受水走水, はまがーうきんじゅはいんじゅ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsudu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (あまつづてんつぎうたき): In {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ruins * Tamagusuku Nunduchi (玉城祝女殿内, たまぐすくぬんどぅち): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Shichinbaru Jingaa (志堅原仁川, しちんばるじんがー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku
=== Nakijin-nobori Utaki (Nakijin Ascension Utaki) === The Nakijin-nobori (なきじんぬぶい) pilgrimage is a sacred journey centered on utaki in the Nakijin region. It is primarily conducted by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). The origins are unclear, but Nakijin, the former capital of the Northern Kingdom (Hokuzan), holds significant historical importance as the birthplace of many Ryukyuan noble lineages. The route and utaki visited vary by clan, but the main sites are:
* Karaukā (カラウカー): Inside {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Hino-kami no Hokora (火の神の祠): Inside Nakijin Castle * Tenchigi Utaki (テンチギの御嶽, also called Kanahiyabu): The second utaki created at Nakijin * Soitsugi Utaki (ソイツギの御嶽): Inside Nakijin Castle * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Inside Nakijin Castle * Aoriyahe Noro Nunduchi (阿応理屋恵祝女殿内, あおりやへのろどぅんち): In {{ill|Nakijin Village|ja|今帰仁村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Nakijin Noro Nunduchi (今帰仁祝女殿内, なきじんのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Tumu no Kane Noro Hino-kami (供のカネー祝女火の神, とぅむなはーにーのろひぬかん): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Oyagaa (今泊の親川, えーがー): Nakijin Village * Nakagusuku Noro Nunduchi (中城祝女殿内, なかぐすくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Tsuya-guchi-baka (今泊の津屋口墓, ちぇーぐちばか): Nakijin Village * Shoshi Akaubaka (諸志の赤御墓, あかうばか): Nakijin Village * Ichigusuku Baka (池城墓, いちぐすくばか): Nakijin Village * Ōnishi Baka (大北墓, うーにしばか, also called Aji Ubaka): Nakijin Village * Momujana Baka (百按司墓, むむじゃなばか): Nakijin Village * Tiragama (ティラガマ): Nakijin Village * Jitchaku Noro Nunduchi (勢理客祝女殿内, じっちゃくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village
=== Sakishima Islands Utaki === The {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which include the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, are home to many ancient sacred sites predating Ryukyuan control. In the Yaeyama Islands, utaki are often called "on" or "wan." Below are some notable examples:
==== Miyako Islands ==== [[File:Miyako harimizu utaki.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ぴゃるみずうたき, はりみずうたき) : [[Miyakojima]] ({{ill|Miyakojima City|ja|宮古島市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). This utaki is dedicated to Koitsuno (古意角) and Koitama (姑依玉), the deities who created Miyako Island. Other deities include the Ryūgū-shin (Dragon Palace God) and the island guardian deity Kokatamotenfū. The surrounding stone walls were built by {{ill|Nakasone Tuyumya|ja|仲宗根豊見親|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to commemorate his victory in the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in 1500. ; Shimajiri Motoshima (島尻元島) : Miyakojima City, Hirara Shimajiri. The site is central to the unique local festival {{ill|Paantu|ja|パーントゥ・プナハ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; Ūparu Utaki (大主御嶽, ウパルズ御嶽, ナナムイ) : {{ill|Ikema Island|ja|池間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyakojima City). Also known as Ōnushi Shrine, this utaki enshrines Uraserikutamenauno Manus, the guardian deity of Ikema people. Immigrants from Ikema established related utaki on {{ill|Irabu Island|ja|伊良部島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Nishihara.
==== Yaeyama Islands ==== [[File:Misaki-On Ishigakijima01s3s4592.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Maitsuba Utaki|ja|真乙姥御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (まいつばおん) : [[Ishigaki Island]] ({{ill|Ishigaki City|ja|石垣市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to a priestess who played a role in the suppression of the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (みしゃぎおん) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). It is a designated {{ill|Cultural Property of Okinawa Prefecture|ja|沖縄県指定文化財一覧|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Ninibushi Utaki|ja|群星御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (んにぶしおん, んにぶしうたき) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). Center of the festival {{ill|Mayunganaashi|ja|マユンガナシ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Nishitō Utaki|ja|西塘御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (にしとうおん) : [[Taketomi Island]] ({{ill|Taketomi Town|ja|竹富町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to {{ill|Nishitō|ja|西塘|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a Yaeyama lord, and designated an Okinawa Prefectural Historic Site. ; {{ill|Kuninaka Utaki|ja|国仲御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふいなーおん, くになかうたき) : Taketomi Island. It is the only utaki in Yaeyama directly connected to the Ryukyu royal family, having received a deity from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Sanri Utaki|ja|三離御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふなふら, みちゃーりおん, さんりうたき) : [[Iriomote Island]] (Taketomi Town, Komi). It shares significance with {{ill|Akamata-Kuromata Festival|ja|アカマタ・クロマタ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Toyama Utaki|ja|十山御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (とぅやまうがん) : [[Yonaguni Island]] ({{ill|Yonaguni Town|ja|与那国町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sonai|ja|祖納|qq=draft|qq=draft}}).
=== Amami Islands === The {{ill|Amami Islands|ja|奄美群島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also had a {{ill|Noro (priestess)|lt=Noro system|ja|ノロ制度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, but there were no {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|qq=draft|qq=draft}} specifically called "utaki" (御嶽). However, sacred sites similar to {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, known as {{ill|Amandee|ja|アマンデー|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (奄美嶽, 海見嶽), do exist. Other sacred places include mountains known as "Ogami-yama" (拝み山) and rock formations called "Tategami" (立神).
Many sites with names like {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine|ja|厳島神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Takachiho Shrine|ja|高千穂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are believed to be utaki-style places of worship rather than standard Shinto shrines. It is thought that these sacred places were converted into Shinto shrines during the rule of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.

{{infobox religious building |name=Utaki }} {{Short description|Sacred place in Ryukyuan religion}} {{Unreferenced stub|auto=yes|date=December 2009}} {{For|the album by [[Misako Odani]] of the same name|Utaki (album)}} [[Image:Sefautaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|Sefa-utaki]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽) is an [[Okinawan language|Okinawan]] term for a sacred place, often a grove, cave, or mountain. They are central to the [[Ryukyuan religion]] and the former [[Noro (priestess)|noro priestess]] system. Although the term ''utaki'' is used throughout the [[Ryukyu Islands]], the terms ''suku'' and ''on'' are heard in the [[Miyako-jima|Miyako]] and [[Yaeyama Islands|Yaeyama]] regions respectively. Utaki are usually located on the outskirts of villages and are places for the veneration of gods and ancestors. Most [[gusuku]] have places of worship, and it is theorized that the origins of both ''gusuku'' and ''utaki'' are closely related.
==Overview==
==Important Utaki== * [[Biinudaki]] ([[弁ヶ嶽]]), [[Naha, Okinawa|Naha]] * [[Misaki-on]] ([[美崎御嶽]]), [[Ishigaki, Okinawa|Ishigaki]] * [[Miyatori-on]] (宮鳥御嶽), [[Nago, Okinawa|Nago]] * [[Pyarumizu-utaki]] (漲水御嶽), [[Miyakojima, Okinawa|Miyako]] * [[Sefa-utaki]] (斎場御嶽), [[Nanjo, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * [[Sunuhyan-utaki]] ([[園比屋武御嶽]]), Naha * [[Tohaya-uganju]] ([[渡波屋拝所]]), Nago * [[Tsunoji-utaki]] ([[ツノジ御嶽]]), Miyako * [[Upugusuku-utaki]] ([[大城御嶽]]), Miyako
{{Source|date=November 6, 2013 (Wed) 01:27 (UTC)}} [[File:Sangui (Triangle Rock) of Sefa-Utaki.jpg|200px|right|thumb|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Sangui (Sangūi)]] '''Utaki''' (御嶽, '''Utaki''') is a sacred site for rituals in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, also known as "Kusatimui" (腰当森) or "Ogami-yama" (拝み山).
== Overview == Utaki is a general term for sacred sites in the {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}} established during the {{ill|Ryukyu Kingdom|ja|琉球王国|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ({{ill|Second Shō dynasty|ja|第二尚氏|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Before this, various regional names existed. The term "Utaki" is primarily used on {{ill|Okinawa Island|ja|沖縄本島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and surrounding islands, but other areas have unique names: - {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: "Suku" (すく) - {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: ** "On" (おん) on {{ill|Ishigaki Island|ja|石垣島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Taketomi Island|ja|竹富島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Ugan" (うがん) on {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Iriomote Island|ja|西表島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Wan" (わん) on {{ill|Kuroshima|ja|黒島 (沖縄県竹富町)|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Kohama Island|ja|小浜島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Aragusuku Island|ja|新城島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ** "Waa" (わー) on {{ill|Hateruma Island|ja|波照間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}
=== Position in Belief === Utaki are sites where deities from Ryukyuan mythology reside or visit, and they are centers of ancestor worship. They remain important places of worship, believed to protect the region. Since women traditionally serve as priests in {{ill|Ryukyuan religion|ja|琉球神道|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, Utaki were strictly {{ill|Nyonin_Kinsei#Danshi_Kinsei_(Men_are_forbidden)|ja|男子禁制|lt=Danshi Kinsei (Men are forbidden)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} during the kingdom era. Even today, many allow only limited male access.
=== Form and Structure === [[File:Utaki.JPG|right|thumb|An Utaki at {{ill|Okinawa Commemorative National Government Park|ja|国営沖縄記念公園|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] Utaki are often natural spaces, such as forests, springs, or rivers; some encompass entire islands. Many have a stone monument called "Ibe" or "Ibi-ishi," marking the site where a deity is believed to descend. Although not originally considered sacred objects, some are now treated as such. In the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, it is common for Utaki to be established on the tombs of past {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, revered as guardian deities.
Large Utaki may include spaces called "Kami-ashagi" (神あしゃぎ, 神あさげ), meaning "God's resting place," where songs and dances are performed to welcome the gods. The term originates from "Kami-ashi-age," meaning a place where the gods 'raise their feet' (sit down).
==== Torii at Utaki and Gusuku ==== [[Torii]] gates, commonly associated with Shinto shrines, are found at the entrances of some Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) in modern Okinawa. However, torii were not part of traditional Ryukyuan Utaki. The notable exception was {{ill|Naminoue Shrine|ja|波上宮|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which included torii from its inception during King {{ill|Satto|ja|察度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s era when Shinto deities were enshrined.
The presence of torii is attributed to the [[Japanization|kōminka policy]] following the {{ill|Ryukyu Disposition|ja|琉球処分|qq=draft|qq=draft}} after the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|ja|明治維新|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Under initiatives like the "One Village, One Shrine" policy, many Utaki and {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} were converted into Shinto shrines.<ref>{{Cite journal|author=Junhito Kaji|title=History and Uniqueness of Okinawan Shrines|journal=Nihon Jomin Bunka Kenkyujo|volume=16|year=2018|pages=37-68|url=https://kanagawa-u.repo.nii.ac.jp/records/12658}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=Was Sefa-utaki almost turned into a shrine? – Nanjō Digital Archive|url=https://nanjo-archive.jp/feature/615/|accessdate=2023-06-02}}</ref>
For example, at {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a torii was installed in 1930 (Shōwa 5) but was removed in 2003 (Heisei 15) after the site was designated a component of the [[UNESCO World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage]]-listed "{{ill|Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu|ja|琉球王国のグスク及び関連遺産群|qq=draft|qq=draft}}," to restore its original landscape.
However, torii installed post-annexation remain at sites like {{ill|Nago Castle|ja|名護城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Tana Shrine|ja|田名神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Iheya Island|ja|伊平屋島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, and {{ill|Arahari Utaki|ja|阿良御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} on {{ill|Ie Island|ja|伊江島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. In the {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyako and Yaeyama), most torii remain intact. == Origins == [[File:Ufuuri.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ufugui (大庫理)]] It is widely believed that Utaki were originally sites of ancient settlements. This theory is supported by numerous discoveries of {{ill|Human remains|ja|遺骨|qq=draft|qq=draft}} near Utaki, indicating their close ties to {{ill|Ancestor worship|ja|祖先崇拝|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Additionally, many rivers and springs are considered Utaki or sacred spaces of equal importance, as ancient societies revered water sources due to Okinawa’s porous {{ill|Ryukyu limestone|ja|琉球石灰岩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which made water precious and sacred.<ref name=":0">[https://ja.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=%E5%BE%A1%E5%B6%BD_(%E6%B2%96%E7%B8%84)&oldid=103787365 Ontake (Okinawa) - Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia]</ref>
Many {{ill|Gusuku|ja|グスク|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (castles) feature {{ill|Haisho#Uganju|lt=Uganju (place of worship)|ja|拝所|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. This has led some scholars to argue that Gusuku were originally settlements centered around Utaki, which later developed into fortresses. Certain castles, such as {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, were themselves regarded as Utaki.<ref name=":0" />
== Modern Status == Ryukyuan faith remains deeply rooted in the local community, with many Utaki still serving as vital spiritual centers, often maintained by the community or female priests known as {{ill|Noro (priestess)|ja|ノロ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. Some Utaki, like {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, have become popular tourist attractions, though these are rare examples. Most remain primarily places of local worship and pilgrimage, such as those visited during the {{ill|Agari-umai|ja|東御廻り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} or {{ill|Nakijin-nubui|ja|今帰仁上り|qq=draft|qq=draft}} pilgrimages.
However, some Utaki have been destroyed or restricted due to {{ill|United States military occupation of Okinawa|ja|アメリカ合衆国による沖縄統治|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, archaeological excavations, or development projects. For example, several Utaki within the {{ill|Shuri Castle|ja|首里城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} grounds were accessible for worshippers before the castle’s reconstruction, but later became off-limits or subject to paid entry.
== Major Utaki == Below is a list of notable Utaki significant in Ryukyuan faith. While most ancient {{ill|Settlements|ja|集落|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in the Ryukyu Kingdom had at least one Utaki, the following are only select prominent examples.
=== Ryukyu Creation Nine Sacred Utaki (琉球開闢九御嶽) === Ryukyuan mythology states that {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the creator deity, was commanded by the {{ill|Sun deity|ja|太陽神|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to create islands, forming Okinawa and establishing nine sacred sites.<ref>"{{ill|Chūzan Seikan|ja|中山世鑑|qq=draft|qq=draft}}"</ref><ref>"Records of {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s Ceremony"</ref> Seven of these remain revered as the most sacred Utaki.
The most significant under the kingdom's theocratic system was {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, where the {{ill|Kikoe-ōgimi|ja|聞得大君|qq=draft|qq=draft}}'s inauguration ceremonies were held. From Sefa-utaki, {{ill|Kudaka Island|ja|久高島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, the landing site of {{ill|Amamikiyo|ja|アマミキヨ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, can be worshipped, although this practice is undocumented in historical records. During royal enthronements, the {{ill|Kimitezuri|ja|君手摩|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ritual required visiting five Utaki, ending at {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
List of the Nine Sacred Utaki in creation order: * {{ill|Asumui Utaki|ja|安須森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Kunigami, Okinawa|Kunigami]] * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: [[Nakijin Castle|Nakijin Gusuku]], [[Nakijin, Okinawa|Nakijin]] * Chinen-mori: [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō]] * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Chinen * {{ill|Yabusatsu Utaki|ja|薮薩御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsuzu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Nanjō, Tamagusuku, within {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * {{ill|Kubou Utaki (Kudaka Island)|ja|クボー御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Kudaka Island * Shurimui Utaki: One of Shuri’s Ten Sacred Sites * {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Shuri Castle
The {{ill|Shuri Madama-mori Utaki|ja|首里真玉森御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} was lost during the Battle of Okinawa and later reconstruction work at Shuri Castle. Entry to its former site is now prohibited. ``` === Higashi-umari Utaki (Eastern Pilgrimage Utaki) === [[File:Sonohyan-utaki.jpeg|right|thumb|{{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, behind the stone gate]] The Higashi-umari (あがりうまーい) is a [[pilgrimage|sacred pilgrimage]] still practiced today, where pilgrims visit utaki in Tamagusuku, Chinen, Sashiki, and Ōzato—regions considered sacred because they lie east of Shuri, the direction where the sun rises and where {{ill|Niraikanai|ja|ニライカナイ|qq=draft|qq=draft}} is believed to exist.
The pilgrimage originated as a ritual of the Ryukyu king, but over time, it spread to the aristocracy and the common people. Today, it is mainly performed by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). Although the pilgrimage route varies slightly by clan, it generally starts from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and follows this order:
* {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (すぬひゃんうたき): Outside [[Shuri Castle]] * Yonabaru Oyagaa (与那原親川, よなばるうぇーがー): [[Yonabaru, Okinawa|Yonabaru Town]] * Udunyama (御殿山, うどぅんやま): Yonabaru Town * Baten Utaki (場天御嶽, ばてぃんうたき): {{ill|Sashiki, Okinawa|ja|佐敷町 (沖縄県)|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in [[Nanjō, Okinawa|Nanjō City]] * Sashiki Uigusuku (佐敷上グスク, さしきうぃぐすく): Nanjō City, Sashiki * Tida Ugā (テダ御川, てぃだうかー): {{ill|Chinen, Okinawa|ja|知念村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (せーふぁうたき): Nanjō City, Chinen * Tomui Utaki (友利ノ御嶽, とむいのたけ): Chinen Gusuku, Nanjō City * Chinen Ukkā (知念大川, ちねんうっかー): Nanjō City, Chinen * Mintongusuku (ミントングスク, みんとぅんぐすく): {{ill|Tamagusuku, Okinawa|ja|玉城村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in Nanjō City * Nakandakari Hīja (仲村渠樋川, なかんだかりひーじゃー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Aihanta Utaki (アイハンタ御嶽, あいはんたうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yabusatsu Utaki (藪薩御嶽, やぶさつうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Yahara Tsukasa (ヤハラヅカサ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Supana Tsukasa (潮花司, すーぱなつかさ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Utaki (浜川御嶽, はまがーうたき): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Hamagawa Ukijuhainju (浜川受水走水, はまがーうきんじゅはいんじゅ): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * {{ill|Amatsudu Tentugi Utaki|ja|雨つづ天つぎ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (あまつづてんつぎうたき): In {{ill|Tamagusuku Castle|ja|玉城城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} ruins * Tamagusuku Nunduchi (玉城祝女殿内, たまぐすくぬんどぅち): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku * Shichinbaru Jingaa (志堅原仁川, しちんばるじんがー): Nanjō City, Tamagusuku
=== Nakijin-nobori Utaki (Nakijin Ascension Utaki) === The Nakijin-nobori (なきじんぬぶい) pilgrimage is a sacred journey centered on utaki in the Nakijin region. It is primarily conducted by {{ill|Monchū|ja|門中|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (patrilineal clans). The origins are unclear, but Nakijin, the former capital of the Northern Kingdom (Hokuzan), holds significant historical importance as the birthplace of many Ryukyuan noble lineages. The route and utaki visited vary by clan, but the main sites are:
* Karaukā (カラウカー): Inside {{ill|Nakijin Castle|ja|今帰仁城|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Hino-kami no Hokora (火の神の祠): Inside Nakijin Castle * Tenchigi Utaki (テンチギの御嶽, also called Kanahiyabu): The second utaki created at Nakijin * Soitsugi Utaki (ソイツギの御嶽): Inside Nakijin Castle * {{ill|Kubou Utaki|ja|クボウ御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}: Inside Nakijin Castle * Aoriyahe Noro Nunduchi (阿応理屋恵祝女殿内, あおりやへのろどぅんち): In {{ill|Nakijin Village|ja|今帰仁村|qq=draft|qq=draft}} * Nakijin Noro Nunduchi (今帰仁祝女殿内, なきじんのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Tumu no Kane Noro Hino-kami (供のカネー祝女火の神, とぅむなはーにーのろひぬかん): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Oyagaa (今泊の親川, えーがー): Nakijin Village * Nakagusuku Noro Nunduchi (中城祝女殿内, なかぐすくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village * Imadomari Tsuya-guchi-baka (今泊の津屋口墓, ちぇーぐちばか): Nakijin Village * Shoshi Akaubaka (諸志の赤御墓, あかうばか): Nakijin Village * Ichigusuku Baka (池城墓, いちぐすくばか): Nakijin Village * Ōnishi Baka (大北墓, うーにしばか, also called Aji Ubaka): Nakijin Village * Momujana Baka (百按司墓, むむじゃなばか): Nakijin Village * Tiragama (ティラガマ): Nakijin Village * Jitchaku Noro Nunduchi (勢理客祝女殿内, じっちゃくのろどぅんち): Nakijin Village
=== Sakishima Islands Utaki === The {{ill|Sakishima Islands|ja|先島諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, which include the {{ill|Miyako Islands|ja|宮古諸島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Yaeyama Islands|ja|八重山列島|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, are home to many ancient sacred sites predating Ryukyuan control. In the Yaeyama Islands, utaki are often called "on" or "wan." Below are some notable examples:
==== Miyako Islands ==== [[File:Miyako harimizu utaki.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Harimizu Utaki|ja|漲水御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ぴゃるみずうたき, はりみずうたき) : [[Miyakojima]] ({{ill|Miyakojima City|ja|宮古島市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). This utaki is dedicated to Koitsuno (古意角) and Koitama (姑依玉), the deities who created Miyako Island. Other deities include the Ryūgū-shin (Dragon Palace God) and the island guardian deity Kokatamotenfū. The surrounding stone walls were built by {{ill|Nakasone Tuyumya|ja|仲宗根豊見親|qq=draft|qq=draft}} to commemorate his victory in the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}} in 1500. ; Shimajiri Motoshima (島尻元島) : Miyakojima City, Hirara Shimajiri. The site is central to the unique local festival {{ill|Paantu|ja|パーントゥ・プナハ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; Ūparu Utaki (大主御嶽, ウパルズ御嶽, ナナムイ) : {{ill|Ikema Island|ja|池間島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (Miyakojima City). Also known as Ōnushi Shrine, this utaki enshrines Uraserikutamenauno Manus, the guardian deity of Ikema people. Immigrants from Ikema established related utaki on {{ill|Irabu Island|ja|伊良部島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and Nishihara.
==== Yaeyama Islands ==== [[File:Misaki-On Ishigakijima01s3s4592.jpg|thumb|right|{{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}]] ; {{ill|Maitsuba Utaki|ja|真乙姥御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (まいつばおん) : [[Ishigaki Island]] ({{ill|Ishigaki City|ja|石垣市|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to a priestess who played a role in the suppression of the {{ill|Oyake Akahachi Rebellion|ja|オヤケアカハチの乱|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Misaki Utaki|ja|美崎御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (みしゃぎおん) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). It is a designated {{ill|Cultural Property of Okinawa Prefecture|ja|沖縄県指定文化財一覧|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Ninibushi Utaki|ja|群星御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (んにぶしおん, んにぶしうたき) : Ishigaki Island (Ishigaki City). Center of the festival {{ill|Mayunganaashi|ja|マユンガナシ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Nishitō Utaki|ja|西塘御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (にしとうおん) : [[Taketomi Island]] ({{ill|Taketomi Town|ja|竹富町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}). Dedicated to {{ill|Nishitō|ja|西塘|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, a Yaeyama lord, and designated an Okinawa Prefectural Historic Site. ; {{ill|Kuninaka Utaki|ja|国仲御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふいなーおん, くになかうたき) : Taketomi Island. It is the only utaki in Yaeyama directly connected to the Ryukyu royal family, having received a deity from {{ill|Sonohyan-utaki|ja|園比屋武御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Sanri Utaki|ja|三離御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (ふなふら, みちゃーりおん, さんりうたき) : [[Iriomote Island]] (Taketomi Town, Komi). It shares significance with {{ill|Akamata-Kuromata Festival|ja|アカマタ・クロマタ|qq=draft|qq=draft}}. ; {{ill|Toyama Utaki|ja|十山御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (とぅやまうがん) : [[Yonaguni Island]] ({{ill|Yonaguni Town|ja|与那国町|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, {{ill|Sonai|ja|祖納|qq=draft|qq=draft}}).
=== Amami Islands === The {{ill|Amami Islands|ja|奄美群島|qq=draft|qq=draft}} also had a {{ill|Noro (priestess)|lt=Noro system|ja|ノロ制度|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, but there were no {{ill|Haisho|ja|拝所|lt=worship sites|qq=draft|qq=draft}} specifically called "utaki" (御嶽). However, sacred sites similar to {{ill|Sefa-utaki|ja|斎場御嶽|qq=draft|qq=draft}}, known as {{ill|Amandee|ja|アマンデー|qq=draft|qq=draft}} (奄美嶽, 海見嶽), do exist. Other sacred places include mountains known as "Ogami-yama" (拝み山) and rock formations called "Tategami" (立神).
Many sites with names like {{ill|Itsukushima Shrine|ja|厳島神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} and {{ill|Takachiho Shrine|ja|高千穂神社|qq=draft|qq=draft}} are believed to be utaki-style places of worship rather than standard Shinto shrines. It is thought that these sacred places were converted into Shinto shrines during the rule of the {{ill|Satsuma Domain|ja|薩摩藩|qq=draft|qq=draft}}.
